title: The browser
intro.1: Google Chrome as an ordinary, maximized window with its tabs and address bar, in a container of its own.
isolation.title: Isolation
isolation.1: No network of its own: its only way out is the session proxy.
isolation.2: No capabilities, a read-only root, by default a uid of its own, a seccomp profile, and the CPU and memory limits you set.
isolation.3: A fresh Chrome profile per session, or a persistent session’s saved one (see Sessions), kept in memory and removed with the session once saved.
chrome-policy.title: Chrome policy
chrome-policy.1: A managed policy is built into the image. Among other things it:
chrome-policy.2: blocks chrome:// pages (except the new tab page and Chrome’s own toolbar), devtools://, file://, view-source:, javascript: and data: addresses;
chrome-policy.3: turns off sign-in, sync, the password manager, autofill, printing, extensions, guest mode and new profiles;
chrome-policy.4: turns off QUIC and Chrome’s own DNS client, so everything goes through the proxy, and sends WebRTC only through it;
chrome-policy.5: saves downloads to the session’s own downloads folder, which streams them to you.
per-session-flags.title: Per-session flags
per-session-flags.4: Opens Chrome’s debugging endpoint on the session’s loopback, for the agent’s browser tools. The agent then runs as Chrome’s uid in Chrome’s network namespace.
per-session-flags.6: The upstream proxy: by its id from the dashboard’s API, by its name from an agent (see Egress proxies).
per-session-flags.8: The page alone on the screen, without tabs or address bar. Only the benchmark profile accepts it; other installations refuse it.
looking-like-an-ordinary.title: Looking like an ordinary browser
looking-like-an-ordinary.1: Chrome runs with a real window, real fonts and WebGL on a software renderer, not headless. Its time zone and languages follow the installation or the egress.
